definition: A Gorn address (Gorn, 1967) is a method of identifying and addressing any node within a tree data structure.
details: This notation is often used for identifying nodes in a parse tree defined by phrase structure rules. The Gorn address is a sequence of zero or more integers conventionally separated by dots, e.g., 0 or 1.0.1. The root which Gorn calls * can be regarded as the empty sequence. And the j {\displaystyle j} -th child of the i {\displaystyle i} -th child has an address i . j {\displaystyle i.j} , counting from 0. It is named after American computer scientist Saul Gorn.

explainer.lead: A Gorn address is a path-style label for locating a node in a tree. It is especially useful in phrase-structure parse trees, where a short sequence such as 1.0.1 identifies one exact node without describing the whole tree.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a tree where every branch has a number, starting at zero. To find one spot, you write down the branch numbers you follow, separated by dots, like directions saying “take branch 1, then branch 0.” The very top needs no directions, so its address is empty.
tiers.practitioner: Gorn addresses can serve as path-based node identifiers when traversing or annotating phrase-structure parse trees. Form a child address by appending .j to its parent’s address, with children numbered from 0, and treat the root as the empty sequence rather than address 0. Common pitfalls are off-by-one numbering and treating the dotted notation as a decimal number.
tiers.paperLevel: Introduced by Saul Gorn (Gorn, 1967), the notation assigns the root, denoted *, the empty address. If a node has address a, its j-th child has address a.j, with child indices counted from 0; thus an address is a sequence of zero or more integers conventionally separated by dots. The address records a structural path, not node labels or the phrase-structure rules that generated the tree.

explainer.example: From the root, take child 1, then that node’s child 0, then that node’s child 1; the destination has Gorn address 1.0.1. The root’s child 0 has address 0, while the root itself has the empty address.

usedIn.name: Phrase-structure parsing
usedIn.detail: Identifies individual nodes in parse trees defined by phrase-structure rules.

usedIn.name: Tree data structures
usedIn.detail: Provides a path-based way to identify and address any node by its sequence of child indices.

explainer.intuition: Think of an address as directions from the root: each integer says which numbered child to visit next. Following the whole sequence leads to one particular node.
howItWorks: Start at the root, which Gorn calls *; its address is the empty sequence.
To address the j-th child of a node with address i, append j to form i.j.
Read a dotted address from left to right, following one child index at a time.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives a compact, unambiguous way to refer to a node’s position in a tree. In parse trees, that makes a particular structural location easy to identify using only child positions.
misconceptions: Address 0 is not the root; it is the root’s first child, while the root has the empty address.
The dots separate path steps; 1.0.1 is not a decimal number.

diagram.caption: Each address records the zero-based child choices taken from the root.
